families.s: HSE health-and-safety management for retail businesses
families.t: employer duties, policy, risk assessment, consultation, training, facilities, insurance, small business and review
f: Health and safety law applies to retail businesses regardless of size.
Employers and self-employed retailers are responsible for controlling work risks.
Businesses should decide who will help with health and safety duties.
A health and safety policy may be required and should reflect the business.
Retailers should assess and manage workplace risks.
Employees should be consulted and provided with information and training.
Suitable workplace facilities and required insurance arrangements should be provided.
Specific retail activities may require controls beyond the basic management system.
families.g: Retail-management risk depends on premises and activities, workforce and public presence, stock and equipment, deliveries, opening hours, contractors, training and management review.

families.s: HSE manual-handling and musculoskeletal-risk control in retail
families.t: avoidance, assessment, loads, tasks, individual capacity, environment, posture, work organisation, handling aids and early reporting
f: Retail employers must manage risks of musculoskeletal injury to workers.
Assessment should consider all tasks rather than isolated lifts.
Individual capacity should be considered.
Loads and the work environment are core assessment factors.
Awkward postures, work organisation and vibration may contribute to risk.
Hazardous manual handling should be avoided where reasonably practicable.
Unavoidable handling should be assessed and effective controls implemented.
Handling aids, worker involvement, training and early reporting can reduce harm.
families.g: Retail manual-handling risk depends on load and frequency, posture and reach, pushing and pulling, storage and delivery layout, equipment, pace, individual capability and work organisation.

families.s: HSE prevention of musculoskeletal disorders at retail checkouts
families.t: checkout design, scanning, reach, posture, repetition, seating, foot support, job rotation, breaks and worker involvement
f: Checkout and till work can cause aches, pains and musculoskeletal disorders.
Assessment should examine the work performed at points of sale.
The position and reach to goods, scanner, keyboard, cash drawer and bags affect risk.
Repeated movements and sustained awkward postures should be reduced.
Workstation and seating should accommodate the worker and task.
Foot support and sufficient leg room can improve posture where appropriate.
Work organisation, breaks and task variation can reduce prolonged repetition.
Workers and safety representatives should be involved in identifying practical improvements.
families.g: Checkout risk depends on workstation layout and adjustability, product size and flow, reach and repetition, posture and seating, shift length, breaks, staffing and individual needs.

families.s: HSE prevention of slips and trips in retail premises
families.t: wet floors, spills, contamination, cleaning, cables, public areas, flooring, footwear, monitoring and prompt response
f: Slips and trips are the single most common cause of major injury in retail.
Smooth floors left wet after cleaning are a common cause.
Spills should be cleaned promptly and effectively.
Floors should be kept free from contamination.
Cleaning itself can create risks for cleaners and people entering the area.
Vacuum and floor-machine cables can create trip hazards.
An effective cleaning regime should identify problem areas, act on findings and check effectiveness.
Controls should protect employees, visitors and members of the public.
families.g: Retail slip risk depends on floor and contaminant, cleaning and drying, footwear, cables and displays, customer traffic, entrances, lighting, maintenance and monitoring.

families.s: HSE workplace-transport controls for retail premises and deliveries
families.t: site separation, routes, surfaces, speed, reversing, drivers, contractors, vehicle selection, maintenance and visiting drivers
f: Retailers must assess risks from vehicle movements to workers and members of the public.
Pedestrians and vehicles should be adequately separated where routes are shared.
Driving surfaces should be suitable for their purpose.
Vehicle speed should be controlled.
Reversing should be avoided where possible and controlled where unavoidable.
Drivers should receive induction and training for company procedures and risks.
Contractor competence and fitness should be assessed.
Vehicles should be suitable, inspected, maintained and repaired, and visiting-driver arrangements coordinated.
families.g: Retail transport risk depends on site layout and public access, deliveries and timing, vehicle and load, visibility and reversing, route and surface, driver competence, contractors and coordination.
